messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 46
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Police
  pcl5: 69

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Threat: Startle Response: Feeling jumpy or easily startled, Physical Reactivity: Having strong physical reactions when something reminded you of the stressful experience, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Overwhelm on Recall: When the memory returns I feel so overwhelmed by emotion that I have to stop, Nonverbal Memory: I can't seem to put the frightening event into words., Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Kofi Mensah is a 46-year-old Ghanaian-American man who works as a curriculum designer for a mid-sized educational nonprofit in Atlanta. He has been married for seventeen years, and until recently, colleagues described him as methodical, warm, and unflappable — the kind of person who could sit through a contentious curriculum review meeting and leave everyone feeling heard. He presented for therapy eight months after an encounter with police that he still cannot fully narrate, even to himself.

The incident occurred on a Tuesday evening last spring. Kofi had stayed late at the office and was walking to his car in the parking structure when two officers responding to an unrelated call in the building approached him at speed, weapons drawn, ordering him to the ground. He was face-down on the concrete for what he later learned was eleven minutes before the situation was clarified. No charges were filed; no formal record of the encounter exists beyond an incident log. What exists, instead, is what those eleven minutes left behind.

In the weeks that followed, Kofi noticed things he could not easily explain to his wife, Abena. He would be standing at the kitchen counter and feel a sudden, full-body lurch at the sound of a door slamming two floors up in their building — heart hammering, hands braced against the counter's edge before he had any conscious thought. At work, the open-plan office that had never bothered him became something he moved through differently. He began positioning himself so that he could see both entry points from his desk. He watched the door when colleagues entered. He was not sure what he was watching for, exactly, but the watching felt necessary in a way he could not argue himself out of.

What troubled Kofi most, and what brought a particular quality of shame into the room during intake, was that he could not tell his story. When Abena gently asked what had happened, he found that the words were not available to him. He knew something had happened. He carried it in his body — in the way his chest tightened when he saw a police cruiser idling at an intersection, in the way his legs went briefly unreliable when a uniformed security guard crossed his path in the lobby of his building. The physical reactions arrived with complete authority: a cold sweat, a constriction in his throat, a sudden heaviness in his limbs. But when he reached for the narrative, for the sequence of events that would let him explain himself to his wife or to himself, it dissolved. He had come to believe that the absence of words meant something was fundamentally wrong with him — that a man who could not account for his own experience was a man who could not be trusted to hold himself together.

There were also moments that arrived without any image at all. He might be reviewing a curriculum draft, reading about civic education of all things, and a wave of terror would move through him — complete, recognizable, and attached to nothing he could see. When this happened he had to stop working. He would close his laptop and sit very still, waiting for it to pass, and afterward he felt wrung out in a way that a full night's sleep did not repair. He had begun declining collaborative projects that required him to be present in rooms he could not easily exit, and his supervisor had noticed. A mentorship role he had been offered — one he had genuinely wanted — he quietly let lapse, offering no explanation.

Kofi finally called a therapist after his wife found him sitting on the bathroom floor at two in the morning, unable to say why. He told her he thought he needed to talk to someone. What he did not say, because he was not sure he could survive saying it, was that he was frightened that what happened to him in that parking structure had changed something permanent — that the man who had been steady and present for his family, for his work, for himself, might not be fully retrievable. What he was most hoping, he said at the end of his first session, was to be able to explain it. To find, somewhere, the words.
